cases.abstract: Low-rank adaptation compresses weight updates but leaves magnitude and direction to be learned through the same factors. A VL-BART checkpoint analysis finds these changes positively correlated with LoRA and negatively correlated with full fine-tuning, motivating separate control of the two components. Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) learns column magnitudes independently while applying low-rank updates to normalized directions; its adapted weights can be merged for inference. On eight commonsense benchmarks with pooled training data, LLaMA-7B reaches 78.4% average accuracy versus 74.7% for the published LoRA baseline, using 0.84% versus 0.83% trainable parameters. DoRA retains the baseline rank but adjusts the learning rate. Halving its rank still yields 77.5% accuracy with a 0.43% trainable fraction. Image- and video-text evaluations also improve over LoRA, although the video-task aggregate remains below full fine-tuning. Detaching the normalization denominator reduces training memory relative to unmodified DoRA with small reported score changes. The findings make the update parameterization, not only its rank, a practical consideration in the tested fine-tuning settings.
cases.methods: A low-rank additive update normally determines both the length and direction of each weight column. DoRA separates these roles: each column is a learned magnitude multiplying the normalized column of W0 + BA, where W0 is frozen and A and B are trainable low-rank factors. Magnitudes start at the pretrained column norms, and initializing B to zero preserves the original weights before adaptation. Normalization prevents the factors from directly setting column length, leaving that control to a small magnitude vector rather than a dense trainable matrix. Exact differentiation projects directional gradients orthogonally to the current column direction. The evaluated implementation instead detaches the normalization denominator during backpropagation to reduce memory. It still recomputes the norm as the factors change, preserving the forward parameterization, but omits the norm derivative. Directional learning therefore uses a scaled gradient rather than inheriting the exact projection.
cases.results: The LLaMA-7B rank sweep tests whether DoRA's gains require a larger adapter. Under the reported training recipes, rank-8 DoRA achieves 77.9% average commonsense accuracy versus 40.7% for rank-8 LoRA, with trainable fractions of 0.22% and 0.21%, respectively. It also exceeds rank-32 LoRA's 74.7%, showing that a smaller directional-update rank can suffice in this setting. Rank sensitivity remains: DoRA scores 61.9% at rank 4 and 72.1% at rank 64, versus 78.4% at rank 32. The gain therefore does not imply that expanding the adapter will improve accuracy. Multimodal evaluation also distinguishes improvement over LoRA from recovery of full fine-tuning. On VL-BART video tasks, DoRA raises the reported aggregate from LoRA's 83.5 to 85.4 but remains below full fine-tuning's 87.5. It matches or slightly exceeds full fine-tuning on three tasks, while trailing on YC2C captioning. Because the aggregate mixes question-answering and captioning metrics, the increase is a benchmark-level score gain, not a percentage-point accuracy gain.
cases.notes: Abstract: Sections 3.2-4.1 motivate separate magnitude control without isolating the cause of accuracy gains. Methods: Eq. 5 assigns column length to the magnitude scalar; Eq. 11 drops the projection term in Eq. 6. Results: Table 15 tests the accuracy-parameter tradeoff and retains rank sensitivity; Table 3 identifies the remaining full-tuning gap. Commonsense and VL-BART baselines come from prior work; DoRA learning rates can differ. Numerical claims follow tables: halved-rank LLaMA-13B gains 0.3 points, not the narrative's one point. Table 7 is a separate overhead ablation and is not combined with Table 1.

cases.abstract: GaLore reduces optimizer-state memory by compressing gradients rather than factorizing the weights being trained. Updates are optimized in a low-rank gradient subspace and expanded onto dense weights; refreshing the basis lets accumulated changes extend beyond any single subspace. For specified gradient forms, the analysis bounds gradient stable rank and gives conditional projected-gradient contraction with fixed projections and an identity gradient regularizer. In C4 pretraining with equal learning-rate search budgets, a 1B model reaches validation perplexity 15.64 versus 15.56 for full-rank Adam and 19.21 for rank-matched LoRA. At 7B, a single distributed comparison without hyperparameter tuning reaches 14.65 versus 14.61 for 8-bit Adam after 19.7 billion tokens. Separate single-device profiling combines projection, 8-bit optimization, and per-layer updates to fit 7B training within 22.0 GB at a 256-token batch, without offloading or checkpointing. The tested implementation also lowers 1B throughput relative to 8-bit Adam. GaLore thus supports dense-weight training under tighter memory budgets, with a throughput cost in the evaluated implementation.
cases.methods: Adam's two moment matrices normally match the weight matrix in size, making gradient statistics a substantial memory cost. For a weight matrix with m <= n, GaLore takes the leading r left singular vectors of its gradient G as a projection P and forms R = P^T G. Adam stores and normalizes its moments in this r-by-n space instead of the original m-by-n space; a scaled update is then lifted through P and applied directly to the dense weights. Periodically recomputing P lets successive updates explore different subspaces without enlarging the moment arrays. Infrequent refreshes can miss useful directions, whereas frequent refreshes add decomposition work and can misalign accumulated statistics. For the specified gradient form, the theorem gives projected-gradient contraction with fixed projections, Lipschitz continuity, bounded weights, a contraction condition, and an identity gradient regularizer. This is not a convergence guarantee for periodically refreshed Adam.
cases.results: With a 256-token batch and no checkpointing or offloading, single-device 7B profiling measures 22.0 GB for 8-bit GaLore, 63.3% below BF16 Adam and 52.3% below 8-bit Adam. This saving combines compressed optimizer states with per-layer updates that avoid retaining all gradients; it cannot be attributed to projection alone. Model quality was assessed separately: a single 7B trial on 64 A100 GPUs reached validation perplexity 14.65 versus 14.61 for 8-bit Adam after 19.7 billion tokens. That comparison shows close observed performance, not statistical equivalence or completed pretraining on a consumer GPU. The matched 1B throughput measurements identify a practical cost. With per-layer updates and a 256-token batch, GaLore processes 1019.63 tokens per second, compared with 1205.31 for 8-bit Adam. These measurements support GaLore when memory is the binding constraint, while showing that reduced storage does not itself imply faster training.
cases.notes: Abstract: Table 2 supports the dense-weight pretraining comparison under equal learning-rate search budgets. Methods: Algorithm 2 explains compact moment storage; Theorem 3.8 requires its gradient form, Lipschitz continuity, bounded weights, fixed projections, an identity gradient regularizer, and a contraction condition. It does not prove convergence of refreshed Adam or global loss convergence. Results: Section 5.5 supplies measured 7B memory, Table 3 supplies separate distributed quality, and Table 11 supplies matched layerwise throughput. Table 2 memory is a parameter-plus-optimizer estimate, not measured total usage. Conflicting smaller-model token counts in Tables 2 and 5 remain omitted.
